passage:
Most roads are built from asphalt, a mixture of stone and a thick black substance left over from refining oil. Producing it requires a great deal of energy, and the world is running short of the sand and gravel that go into it. At the same time, governments everywhere are struggling to dispose of waste plastic. A number of engineers have asked an obvious question: why not combine the two problems?

The method is simpler than it sounds. Waste plastic is shredded into small flakes and added to the hot stone before the asphalt binder is mixed in. The plastic melts and coats the stones, and the binder is then added as usual. Roughly one tenth of the binder can be replaced this way.

Trials in India, Britain and Australia suggest several advantages. Roads containing plastic have shown better resistance to water, which is the main cause of potholes. They also appear to soften less in very hot weather. Each kilometre of such road uses the equivalent of hundreds of thousands of plastic bags that would otherwise be buried or burned.

Critics raise a serious objection. As tyres wear the surface away, the plastic does not disappear; it breaks into tiny fragments that wash into rivers and eventually the sea. Whether plastic roads shed more of these particles than ordinary ones is still being measured, and the results so far disagree with one another.

For now the technology remains a small part of road building. Its future depends less on engineering than on whether that question about fragments can be answered convincingly.
